_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order). Test 4 mixes detail, reference ('this'), opinion and a final inference about the person. Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page and by Full test 4.
title: Between the lines
subtitle: Lucía Ferro writes the subtitles for foreign films. Ben Archer watched her spend a morning on ninety seconds of dialogue.

cards.text: Lucía Ferro has watched the same ninety-second scene forty-one times this morning, and she has not finished with it yet. On her screen, two elderly brothers are arguing in a kitchen in Naples, both talking at once. The problem, she explains, is not understanding what they say. It is deciding what to leave out. 'People read more slowly than actors speak,' she says. 'If I give you every word, you'll spend the whole scene reading and never see their faces. And their faces are the point.'
cards.question: What is the main difficulty Lucía describes with the scene?
choices: understanding the actors' regional accent
choosing which parts of the dialogue not to include
deciding which brother the audience should follow
finishing the work before her deadline
cards.highlight: It is deciding what to leave out.
cards.why: 'The problem… is not understanding what they say. It is deciding what to leave out.' A is the problem she rules out.

cards.text: She came to the job almost by accident. After a degree in modern languages she spent three years teaching English in Bologna, where her students persuaded her to run an evening film club. Each week she would show a British film and prepare her own Italian subtitles, partly to save money and partly, she admits, to show off. A visiting producer saw one of the screenings and asked who had done the translation. 'I assumed I was in trouble,' she says. 'Actually, he was offering me a job.'
cards.question: What does Lucía suggest about the subtitles she made for the film club?
choices: They were mainly a way of improving her Italian.
They were paid for by her students.
They were meant to attract the attention of producers.
They were partly intended to impress other people.
cards.highlight: partly, she admits, to show off
cards.why: She made them 'partly to save money and partly… to show off'. The producer's visit was luck: she 'assumed I was in trouble', so C is wrong.

cards.text: Twenty years later, Lucía works from a small room at the top of her house in Bristol, with two screens, a keyboard and a large dictionary she rarely opens. Most of her work arrives as digital files with impossible deadlines: a feature film in a week is normal, and she has done one in three days. She does not complain about this. What she does object to is the growing habit of producing a quick machine translation first and paying a human only to correct it. 'It's like asking a chef to fix a microwave meal,' she says. 'You can do it, but you can't be proud of the result.'
cards.question: What does 'this' refer to in 'She does not complain about this'?
choices: the size of the room she works in
the use of machine translation
the speed at which she is expected to work
the way the films are sent to her
cards.highlight: a feature film in a week is normal, and she has done one in three days
cards.why: 'This' points back to the 'impossible deadlines' just described. Machine translation is what she DOES object to, in the next sentence.

cards.text: The chef comparison is one she returns to often. A good subtitle, she argues, is a translation not of words but of effect. If a joke depends on a play on words that does not exist in English, she will replace it with a different joke that gets the same laugh in the same place. Purists sometimes accuse her of taking liberties. Her answer is that an audience that does not laugh at a comedy has been given a less accurate version than one that laughs at a slightly different line.
cards.question: What is Lucía's view of changing the jokes in a film?
choices: It can be more faithful to the original than a word-for-word version.
It is only acceptable in films made for children.
It is something she does less often than critics believe.
It sometimes makes audiences laugh in the wrong places.
cards.highlight: an audience that does not laugh at a comedy has been given a less accurate version
cards.why: A silent audience has had 'a less accurate version': the new joke keeps the effect, which is what she means by accuracy. D reverses her point: she keeps 'the same laugh in the same place'.

cards.text: Not every challenge is a matter of language. Lucía once spent two days on a single word: the name of a cake that a grandmother bakes throughout a Portuguese film and which turns out, in the last scene, to explain the whole story. 'I couldn't translate it, I couldn't leave it out, and I couldn't explain it, because a subtitle is two lines, not a footnote.' In the end she kept the original name and added nothing, trusting the film to do the work. Several reviewers mentioned the cake. None of them mentioned the subtitles, which Lucía regards as the highest compliment.
cards.question: Why does Lucía regard it as a compliment that reviewers did not mention the subtitles?
choices: Reviewers usually criticise her work.
It proves that the cake's name was translated correctly.
She had added a note to explain the word.
Good subtitles should not draw attention to themselves.
cards.highlight: None of them mentioned the subtitles, which Lucía regards as the highest compliment.
cards.why: She trusted 'the film to do the work': the reviewers noticed the cake, not her lines, which is what she wants. She did NOT translate the name or add a note, so B and C are wrong.

cards.text: As I leave, she is back with the brothers in Naples, who are still arguing. She has cut one of them down to four words, and she is not happy about it. 'He's the funnier one,' she says, 'so of course he's the one who talks too fast.' She types, deletes, types again, then sits back with her arms folded and stares at the screen, as though the brothers might be persuaded to slow down. Then she plays the scene again, for the forty-second time, and for a moment she laughs out loud, as if she has never seen it before.
cards.question: What does the final paragraph suggest about Lucía?
choices: She finds the work rather repetitive.
She still enjoys the films she works on.
She is satisfied with her solution for the scene.
She would prefer to translate only comedies.
cards.highlight: she laughs out loud, as if she has never seen it before
cards.why: On the forty-second viewing she still 'laughs out loud, as if she has never seen it before'. She is 'not happy' with the cut, so C is wrong.
